wedge.question: My supplier raised prices. Should I pass it on?
wedge.page_title: Shop cost decision — three choices compared
wedge.headline: Your supplier put prices up {shock}%. Should you pass it on?
wedge.hero_lede: Three ways to respond, compared on the same model of your shop and the same assumptions. Only the decision changes between them.
wedge.what_changed: Your supplier put wholesale prices up {shock}%.

world_verdict_labels.C: A 4% rise plus dropping low-margin lines

wedge.unknown_why: A shop's customers can often buy the same item elsewhere, so a price rise costs more orders here than in a trade where people come for you specifically. How much more is the thing nobody has measured for your shop.
wedge.unknown_how: Put prices up on a handful of lines for two weeks and watch what happens to those lines against the rest. Your own numbers from the last time you raised prices work too.

sens_help.low: Loyal customers, an awkward shop to replace, or competitors raising prices too.
sens_help.central: Our judgement: customers who could shop elsewhere, with some effort.
sens_help.high: The research figure for customers who can buy the identical item elsewhere.

wedge.c_card_note: Depends on how much dropping low-margin lines cuts your cost of goods (about {red} points here) and how many {unit} leave with those lines ({loss}%). Neither is measured from your shop.
wedge.chart_lede: Costs take about three weeks to rise — the stock on your shelves was bought at the old price. Customers react to a new price within a week or two.
wedge.sources_note: The research quoted measures customers switching between brands on the same shelf, which is easier than switching shops. It sets the top of the range rather than the middle.
limits_does_not: Know how your individual customers will behave.
Model competitors, marketplaces or search ranking.

wedge.question: تأمین‌کننده قیمت را بالا برده. من هم قیمت را بالا ببرم؟
wedge.page_title: تصمیم هزینه در فروشگاه — مقایسهٔ سه انتخاب
wedge.headline: تأمین‌کننده قیمت را {shock}٪ بالا برده. تو هم بالا ببری؟
wedge.hero_lede: سه راه واکنش، روی یک مدل از فروشگاه خودت و با همان فرض‌ها مقایسه شده‌اند. تنها چیزی که بینشان فرق می‌کند، خودِ تصمیم است.
wedge.what_changed: تأمین‌کننده قیمت عمده را {shock}٪ بالا برده.

world_verdict_labels.C: ۴٪ بالا بردن قیمت همراه با حذف کالاهای کم‌سود

wedge.uncertainty_title: مشتری‌های تو چقدر به قیمت حساس‌اند؟
wedge.unknown_why: مشتری فروشگاه معمولاً همان جنس را جای دیگری هم پیدا می‌کند، پس بالا بردن قیمت اینجا بیشتر از صنف‌هایی که مشتری برای خودِ تو می‌آید سفارش می‌برد. اینکه چقدر بیشتر، برای فروشگاه تو اندازه‌گیری نشده.
wedge.unknown_how: قیمت چند قلم را دو هفته بالا ببر و ببین فروش همان‌ها نسبت به بقیه چه می‌شود. عددهای دفعهٔ قبلی که قیمت را بالا بردی هم کار می‌کند.

sens_help.low: مشتری وفادار، فروشگاهی که جایگزین‌کردنش سخت است، یا رقبایی که آن‌ها هم گران کرده‌اند.
sens_help.central: قضاوت ما: مشتری‌ای که می‌تواند جای دیگری برود، ولی کمی زحمت دارد.
sens_help.high: عدد پژوهشی برای مشتری‌ای که دقیقاً همان جنس را جای دیگر می‌خرد.

wedge.c_card_note: به این بستگی دارد که حذف کالاهای کم‌سود چقدر از قیمت تمام‌شده کم می‌کند (اینجا حدود {red} واحد) و چند {unit} همراه آن کالاها می‌رود ({loss}٪). هیچ‌کدام از فروشگاه تو اندازه‌گیری نشده.
wedge.chart_lede: هزینه‌ها حدود سه هفته طول می‌کشد تا بالا بیاید — جنسی که روی قفسه است با قیمت قبلی خریده شده. مشتری‌ها یکی دو هفته‌ای واکنش نشان می‌دهند.
wedge.sources_note: پژوهشی که نقل شده، جابه‌جا شدن مشتری بین برندهای روی یک قفسه را می‌سنجد، که از عوض‌کردن فروشگاه راحت‌تر است. پس سقف بازه را تعیین می‌کند، نه وسط آن را.
limits_does_not: فروش آیندهٔ تو را پیش‌بینی کند.
رقبا، مارکت‌پلیس‌ها یا رتبهٔ جست‌وجو را مدل کند.
تبلیغات یا کمپین‌ها را مدل کند.

The ranking depends mainly on how much dropping low-margin lines really saves and how price-sensitive customers are. This is sensitivity analysis, not a probability estimate.

assumptions.label: Share of orders on low-margin lines
Price sensitivity of customers
assumptions.note: A 1% price rise eventually reduces orders by this percentage. Low 0.70 / central 1.30 / high 2.60. Only the high setting is a published figure — the brand-level meta-analytic mean, i.e. customers who can buy the identical item elsewhere. The central and low settings are our judgement, set below brand level because changing shop is harder than changing brand. This is the assumption most likely to change the decision.
assumptions.source: No study supports this setting. bijmolt2005 and tellis1988 measure brand switching inside a shop and set the top of the range, not its middle.

assumptions.label: Share of supplier increase reaching your cost of goods
assumptions.note: 100% by definition unless you can substitute cheaper lines, renegotiate, or hold fixed-price contracts (tested at 70%).

assumptions.label: Delay before higher supplier prices reach your costs
assumptions.note: Stock already on the shelf was bought at the old price. Tested over a 10-30 day range; the comparison uses the midpoint. A shop holding more stock than that sees the increase later than this shows.

assumptions.label: How quickly customers react to a price change

map.slow: about two and a half weeks to half-react

assumptions.label: Cost saving from dropping low-margin lines
assumptions.value: 7.5 points off average cost of goods (0.375 per point of low-margin share)
assumptions.note: Assumes low-margin lines carry roughly 2.9x the average cost share, which is close to what makes them low-margin. Tested at half and one-and-a-half times this rate.

value_spec.text: {reduction:g} points off average cost of goods ({trim_effectiveness:.3f} per point of low-margin share)

assumptions.label: Orders lost from dropping those lines
assumptions.note: 0.45 of the cost saving, in points of orders: customers who came for the removed lines and do not substitute. Higher than the cafe's ratio because a shopper who cannot find a specific product is more likely to leave.

assumptions.label: Price rises compared
assumptions.note: The decisions being compared; fixed by the question.

assumptions.label: Comparison horizon
assumptions.note: Long enough for the stock to turn over at the new cost and for most of the customer reaction to land; short enough that rent and wages can be treated as fixed.

assumptions.label: Average order value
assumptions.note: Monthly sales divided by monthly orders.

sources.citation: Bijmolt THA, van Heerde HJ, Pieters RGM. New empirical generalizations on the determinants of price elasticity. Journal of Marketing Research. 2005;42(2):141-156.
sources.population: 1,851 price elasticities from 81 studies, predominantly packaged consumer goods in retail scanner data
sources.limitations: Brand-level in supermarket categories with near-perfect substitutes on the same shelf. It measures switching between brands inside a shop, not switching between shops.
sources.transfer: Used as the upper reference point. For a shop it is the 'my customers can buy the identical thing elsewhere' end of the range; for a cafe it is further away still, and the HIGH setting of 1.60 there is a judgement placed between the food category CI top (1.07) and this mean.

sources.citation: Tellis GJ. The price elasticity of selective demand: a meta-analysis of econometric models of sales. Journal of Marketing Research. 1988;25(4):331-341.
sources.population: 367 price elasticities from roughly 220 brands and markets
sources.limitations: Selective (brand-level) demand, largely goods rather than services, and estimated from studies published up to the mid-1980s. Like Bijmolt it measures brand switching, not store switching.
sources.transfer: A second brand-level reference point for the shop wedge, quoted so the range shown is not resting on a single meta-analysis. It does not establish what happens when one shop raises all of its prices at once.
